strengths: Addresses an important evaluation gap: performance on large, structurally diverse CO instances beyond the small synthetic distributions commonly used in neural optimization.
Provides broad coverage across eight problems, combining established benchmark sources, neural methods, LLM-generated algorithms, and strong classical solvers.

The detailed results expose practically relevant scalability failures. Appendix E also provides useful evidence that classical TSP heuristics can outperform neural methods in both speed and solution quality.
weaknesses: The claimed standardized training comparison is not implemented consistently. Appendix C primarily uses existing checkpoints trained under different protocols, while other models are retrained. This is useful as an off-the-shelf robustness evaluation, but does not isolate the effects of scale, structural distribution shift, training data, and solver design. Matched-distribution controls and adaptation experiments are needed to support broader conclusions about ML limitations.

Reference-solution handling raises validity concerns. Equation 2 assigns a positive gap even when a solver improves on a nonoptimal BKS. Appendix B.4 also removes route-length constraints from eight Golden CVRP instances while retaining website BKS, without establishing that those references correspond to the modified problem. Reference updates and verification against the exact evaluated formulations are necessary.

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the benchmark. Table 1 claims MIS instances approaching eight million nodes, whereas Appendix B.1 describes selecting moderately sized DIMACS clique complements and BHOSLib graphs without explaining this scale. FJSP-hard contains 20 instances in Table 1 but 24 in Appendix B.7. Table 7 marks HGS-hard runtime with a failure indicator; under the stated protocol, one failed instance among ten would already imply an average gap of at least 10%, inconsistent with the reported 6.74%.

The headline LLM improvements are small and lack adequate uncertainty analysis: Self-Refine improves MIS-easy from 1.51% to 1.30%, and FunSearch improves CVRP-hard from 6.74% to 6.52%. The paper does not establish these gains through repeated independent algorithm searches, paired per-instance comparisons, or confidence intervals. Variation across problems is also insufficient evidence for the claimed variability across LLM sampling runs.

The causal interpretations substantially exceed the experiments. A validation-F1 comparison between two STP datasets does not establish a fundamental inability of GNNs to represent global structure; graph size, label balance, nonunique optimal solutions, optimization, and architecture are not controlled. Likewise, attributing LLM performance differences to an absence of internal reasoning is unsupported.

Evaluation does not sufficiently separate failure rates from feasible-solution quality: assigning every failure a 100% gap can dominate averages, yet failure counts and size-stratified results are absent. Runtime reporting also needs clarification: Appendix C says LEHD and DeepACO continue refinement until the time limit, but several reported runtimes are far shorter. Broader quality-versus-time curves would make comparisons more interpretable.

Reproducibility and baseline coverage remain incomplete for a benchmark contribution. The new STP neural baselines lack sufficient architectural and training details, classical solver configurations and random-seed protocols are underspecified, and generic commercial solvers substitute for specialized methods on several tasks without sufficiently establishing competitiveness. The paper also needs a clearer comparison with existing benchmark suites to substantiate its incremental contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation gap: performance on small synthetic instances does not establish practical competitiveness on large or structurally different combinatorial optimization problems.
The evaluation spans eight problem families, multiple neural and LLM-based approaches, and strong classical baselines. This breadth could make the benchmark a useful community resource.

The results document substantial scalability failures and distribution-shift sensitivity. Appendix E also provides a useful comparison showing that classical solvers can deliver strong solutions under short runtime budgets.
The paper includes dataset provenance, implementation details, and initial ablations demonstrating that neural components can improve their underlying classical methods.
weaknesses: The claimed standardized training protocol is not established by the experiments. Sections 2.2 and 2.5 emphasize common training distributions, but Appendix C primarily uses existing checkpoints trained under different original protocols, while Appendix B explicitly omits neural training parameters and dataset sizes. Testing these checkpoints is useful, but without matched retraining or controlled size-versus-structure experiments, the results cannot distinguish limitations of the methods from training-distribution mismatch.

The evaluation protocol and reported runtimes are inconsistent. Appendix C says LEHD reconstruction and DeepACO's HGS decoding continue until the one-hour budget is exhausted, yet their easy-set geometric mean runtimes are 487/893 seconds and 50 seconds, respectively. It is unclear whether these values measure total runtime or time to the best solution. Table 7 also marks HGS-hard as having a feasibility failure, but its 6.74% mean gap over ten instances is incompatible with assigning even one failure a 100% gap. These discrepancies require resolution before the comparisons are reliable.

Reference-solution validity needs stronger treatment. Appendix B.4 removes route-length constraints from eight Golden CVRP instances but still retrieves BKS from CVRPLib without explaining whether those references match the modified problems. Moreover, Equation 2 uses an absolute difference from BKS, so a solution improving a nonoptimal reference receives a positive penalty. The benchmark needs an explicit policy for validating, updating, and scoring reference improvements.

The mechanistic conclusions substantially exceed the evidence. One GNN's low Steiner-node prediction F1 on hypercube instances does not establish a fundamental inability of neural solvers to capture global structure; architecture, optimization, class balance, and ambiguity among alternative optimal solutions are not controlled. Likewise, cross-problem variation among generated algorithms does not establish an absence of internal reasoning in LLMs. These should be framed as hypotheses.

The claimed LLM victories are small and lack adequate uncertainty analysis: Self-Refine improves the easy MIS mean gap from 1.51% to 1.30%, and FunSearch improves hard CVRP from 6.74% to 6.52%. The paper does not report repeated independent agent searches, clearly identify the variation represented by gap error bars, or provide paired per-instance evidence. Consequently, neither reliable superiority nor the claimed run-to-run variability is demonstrated.

Failure-aware averages obscure the causes of poor performance. Assigning timeouts and out-of-memory failures a 100% gap is reasonable for an aggregate benchmark score, but reporting only that score and an asterisk conflates feasibility, scalability, and solution quality. Exact failure counts, quality conditional on feasibility, and results stratified by instance size are needed, especially for the headline hard-TSP gaps.

Benchmark construction and reproducibility remain insufficiently specified. Table 1 lists easy MIS instances reaching roughly eight million nodes, whereas Appendix B.1 describes complementary DIMACS clique graphs without explaining this scale. The hard FJSP set contains 20 instances in Table 1 but 24 in Appendix B.7. The supplied manuscript also lacks usable benchmark/code links and sufficient details for the custom STP models. These gaps are particularly consequential for a paper whose main contribution is a reusable benchmark.

The novelty and realism claims need sharper positioning. Many instances are established competition datasets, and the hard TSP set is explicitly synthetic. Aggregating these resources can be valuable, but the paper does not sufficiently establish its additional capabilities relative to existing benchmarks or justify describing competition provenance as real-world realism.

strengths: Addresses an important evaluation gap: performance on small synthetic instances does not establish practical competitiveness on large, structurally diverse combinatorial optimization problems.

Provides broad coverage across eight problems, multiple neural approaches, three LLM agent frameworks, and strong classical baselines. Including structurally difficult small instances alongside very large instances is valuable.
The detailed results document substantial scalability and feasibility failures. Appendix E also provides useful evidence that classical TSP heuristics remain competitive under short runtime budgets.
The neural-component ablations and qualitative inspection of generated algorithms add useful context beyond aggregate rankings.
weaknesses: Reference-solution validity needs stronger controls. Appendix B.4 removes route-length constraints from eight Golden CVRP instances but retains published BKS without establishing that these references remain appropriate. Equation 2 also penalizes solutions that improve upon a nonoptimal reference because it uses an absolute difference. This is especially problematic where references are merely two-hour Gurobi incumbents.

The claimed LLM improvements lack statistical support. Self-Refine improves MIS-easy from 1.51% to 1.30%, and FunSearch improves CVRP-hard from 6.74% to 6.52%, but independent agent-search repetitions, paired uncertainty estimates, and significance analyses are absent. Aggregate variability across instances cannot establish reproducibility of these small gains.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. Table 7 marks HGS on the ten-instance CVRP-hard set as having a failure, yet reports a 6.74% mean gap; one failure assigned 100% would alone imply a mean of at least 10%. Table 1 lists 20 hard FJSP instances, whereas Appendix B.7 specifies 24. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the benchmark accounting.

The standardized-training claim is not substantiated by the implemented protocol. Appendix C largely reuses checkpoints trained on different original datasets, while Appendix B explicitly omits neural training sizes and generation parameters. Solver versions, classical configurations, random seeds, and the custom STP architecture and training procedure are insufficiently specified.

The experiments conflate size shift, structural shift, training distribution, and resource failures. Reporting failure rates separately from feasible-solution quality, stratifying results by size and structure, and adding controlled adaptation experiments would make the conclusions substantially more informative.

The structural-reasoning claims exceed the evidence. Failure of one GNN setup to predict Steiner nodes on hypercube instances does not establish a fundamental inability of neural solvers to capture global structure; optimization difficulties, label ambiguity, and architectural choices remain uncontrolled. Likewise, cross-task LLM performance differences do not demonstrate an absence of internal reasoning.

The classical comparisons do not consistently establish the state of the art. MDS uses Gurobi without comparison to specialized challenge solvers, and the small CVRP advantage is established only against HGS rather than additional methods suited to these very large instances. Runtime reporting also needs clarification: several methods described as continuing until the one-hour limit have substantially shorter reported runtimes.
